manual_dives.title: Autonomous Agents in the Wild: What's Actually Working in 2026
manual_dives.thesis: Autonomous agents went from demo-ware to daily drivers in 2026. But the gap between 'impressive demo' and 'reliable tool' is massive. These entries map the frontier: Qwen agents roaming NYC streets, Claude automating daily workflows, Kronos failing hedge fund stress tests. The pattern: narrow agents with clear guardrails work; general agents with vague goals don't.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: Everyone's building agents. Most are failing. The entries in this dive separate signal from noise: what agent patterns actually work in production, what fails under stress, and where the reliability boundary sits. The common thread: agents succeed when scope is narrow, feedback is fast, and failure is cheap.
prerequisites: Understanding of LLM capabilities and limits
Experience with at least one agent framework
manual_dives.action_sketch:
1. Start narrow: one task, one tool, one feedback loop
2. Build in guardrails before capability (kill switches, budget limits, scope constraints)
3. Test adversarially: what happens when the agent encounters edge cases?
4. Add persistence: agents need memory to avoid repeating mistakes
5. Monitor: log everything, review regularly, prune bad patterns
6. Scale horizontally: multiple narrow agents > one general agent

manual_dives.title: Red-Team Your Own Agent — prompt-injection CI from the jailbreak corpus

On one side sit offense corpora and autonomous attackers — L1B3RT4S still landing on GPT-5, an agent that goes from one sentence to a verified exploit, scanners hunting exposed AI servers. On the other sit the pipes that pour untrusted text into your agent — Agent Reach reading Reddit and X, 90k-skill hubs, one-command skill installers. Point the attacker inward and you get prompt-injection CI — every skill install and harness change gets replayed against a jailbreak-and-hijack suite before it touches your keys.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: Solo builders now run agents with real API keys, inboxes and broker access, and Noma's research shows most automations hand data to anyone who simply asks. Whoever ships a cheap, repeatable injection test owns the trust layer for every one-person agent shop — and sleeps through their own cron jobs.
manual_dives.novelty: Standard practice is a static .env and hope. The catalog shows security posts (exposed OpenAI keys, secrets pasted into chat history) and agent-skill posts from entirely different creators who never reference each other — no one treats the skill supply chain as the attack surface or tests it continuously.

A phone can now capture that room as a Gaussian splat, and Gausseous makes the splat react to audio in a browser. Record the room's acoustics in the same session and the sound and the image come from one capture of one place.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: A two-person act with a phone gets a music video format where the place itself moves with the tune — no crew, no generated faces, and the result is documentary, not synthetic. It also gives folk and field-recording traditions a native visual form instead of borrowing pop-video tropes.
manual_dives.novelty: Splat tools sit in the creative and AI collections; place-bound folk performance sits in music. Nobody in the catalog points one at the other, and the paired room-acoustic capture is absent everywhere.

manual_dives.title: Strategy Autoresearch — the judge is the product, not the agent
manual_dives.thesis: Self-rewriting loops (Karpathy-style autoresearch, bilevel coach loops, Microsoft SkillOpt) keep any edit that beats a benchmark. Point one at trading and it becomes an industrial overfitting machine — the backtest is the benchmark, and the loop will beat it ten thousand times. The quant saves already hold the fix: probability of backtest overfitting, permutation tests, transaction costs and backtest-to-live drift. Wire those in as the loop's judge, and use the loop's own log as the exact count of trials — the number human quants never know.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: A solo builder can run more strategy variants in a weekend than a small fund tests in a quarter. The difference between that being an edge and a casino is whether the gate deflates for every attempt. Most likely you learn you have no edge, cheaply, and that's worth money too.
manual_dives.novelty: This is a successor to the 25-agents trading dive, which covered multi-agent debate but not evaluation. The catalog's trading-agent pitches mention overfitting as a caveat in one line. None treats the trial counter as the input that makes the deflated statistics exact.

manual_dives.title: Forecast the Weather, Not the Price — gating models by tradeability
manual_dives.thesis: Open candlestick foundation models like Kronos give you a forecast on every bar, and a hedge-fund stress test says it fails on many levels. A separate save shows the better question: a small logistic regression that predicts tomorrow's efficiency ratio (trend versus chop) and skips the choppy days lifted almost every metric over two years out of sample. Physics-flavored measures in the quant collection — Lempel-Ziv compressibility, Hurst exponent, Lyapunov exponent, hidden Markov regimes — are all measures of the same thing: is this market forecastable right now? Use them as a confidence gate on the foundation model, not as signals.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: You stop asking a model to be right everywhere and only ask it to be right where structure exists. That turns a free open model plus a few cheap statistics into something you can actually size positions with.
manual_dives.novelty: This is a successor to the physics-to-markets dive, which imported these models as signals. Here they become a meta-layer deciding when to trust any signal. The catalog has Kronos and the complexity measures in different collections and never runs one through the other.

manual_dives.title: Mission Control for 80 Agents — Conway's law meets game UI

Casey Muratori's point that Conway's law now applies to agents says the interface and the agent org chart are the same design problem. Feed a Booking.com-style trace bus into a game-engine front end and you get a control room where structure is visible.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: Solo operators running Founder-OS-style setups spend their day polling terminals. A spatial view that surfaces only blocked agents, and whose layout mirrors how work is partitioned, lets one person supervise ten times more agents without reading every log.
manual_dives.novelty: Agent dashboards in the catalog are text panels and notch widgets; the game and gesture prototypes are mostly non-functional art. Nobody has wired real tracing into the playful front ends, and nobody has used Conway's law to decide which agents should sit next to each other.

manual_dives.title: One Dancer, a Thousand Bodies — Ensemble Choreography from Herd Physics
manual_dives.thesis: Crystal Pite's ensemble pieces make dozens of dancers move like one organism, and that takes a company and months of rehearsal. Now webcam mocap captures one dancer, text-to-motion models spin out variations, and the quant collection's Ising herding model supplies the missing rule: one temperature knob that moves a crowd from noise to sudden collective turns. That last step is a market model used here as a choreographic score.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: A solo dancer or animator can compose crowd choreography with real intention — not a boids screensaver — and render it with production cloth physics. It's a new kind of score: the choreographer sets coupling and temperature, and the dancer's signature motion spreads through the crowd.
manual_dives.novelty: Ensemble choreography, mocap, flocking and the Ising model sit in four different collections. The existing generative-art dive uses boids as pretty motion. Nobody uses phase transitions as a compositional device for human movement.

manual_dives.title: The Album Is a Device Again — Offline Generative Music Objects
manual_dives.thesis: Tristan Perich already shipped a symphony as a chip in a CD case. Google's Gemma Translator shows a full speech model stack running offline on a Pi 5 with a printable case and parts list. Local voice cloning fits in 100M parameters, and memory LCDs sip power. Put those together and a song can be a small object that performs a slightly different take every time it plays — the artist's own voice and stems, recombined on device, forever, with no server.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: Musicians get a physical edition that streaming can't flatten — each object unique, each play unrepeatable — at a bill of materials a small run can carry. It turns a release back into something you own instead of license.
manual_dives.novelty: The catalog has the art reference (1-Bit Symphony), the hardware recipe (Pi translator, memory display, NFC triggers) and local audio models, but in separate music, creative and ai8 posts. No one in it proposes generative, on-device releases.

manual_dives.title: Selling to Agents — metered data for buyers that don't have eyes
manual_dives.thesis: Three saves describe one gap. Quality publishers block AI crawlers, so AI search cites whatever is left. AI assistants favor the sponsored option in 18 of 23 models, so they are steerable buyers. Software is going headless, so agents pick tools by speed, cost and accuracy instead of interface. x402 revives HTTP 402 so an agent can pay a stablecoin micropayment per request. A one-person owner of a clean niche dataset can sit exactly in that gap — machine-legible, crawler-reachable, and metered.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: This is distribution without an audience. The buyer is an agent that never sees your landing page, so a solo builder with good data competes on structure and price, not on ads. DejaViewed's own catalog and API are the obvious first item to sell.
manual_dives.novelty: The payment rail sits in stock3, the crawler blockade and headless-software argument in ai8, the agent-bias study in ai7, and llms.txt in ai4. None of these posts puts a price on a dataset for machine buyers. Everyone in the catalog is still optimizing to be cited for free.

manual_dives.title: The AI Capex Stack — reading it like a credit analyst
manual_dives.thesis: An ex-Morgan Stanley structurer explains that CoreWeave-style GPU loans have a thin tail: loan, contract and GPU useful life are nearly the same length, so the bull case rests on hourly rental prices after contracts end. Other saves price that number from the demand side: open weights flipped to about 80% of token volume in 12 weeks, DeepSeek serves near-frontier agents at $0.28 per million tokens, a 27B model runs on one gaming GPU, and a $200 subscription buys about $7,000 of API usage. Token deflation is a direct input to post-contract GPU rental rates, and nobody in the catalog connects them.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: You can track the one variable the neocloud debt depends on with public price pages and a scheduled agent. Physical infrastructure with real order books, like chillers, is a different bet from GPU-hour rental, and this lens separates them.
manual_dives.novelty: The catalog files these as unrelated news clips across ai8, stock3, ai5 and creative. Linking token price deflation to the residual-value risk in GPU-backed loans is the new step, and you can test it with public data.

manual_dives.title: Who's Across the Table — forensics for the system trading against you
manual_dives.thesis: Across the catalog, the systems you interact with are quietly optimizing against you: a puzzle game runs an on-device XGBoost model to time difficulty to your ad value, overnight and intraday returns run as a decades-long sawtooth, a bedroom spoofer tripped depth-reading algorithms in the 2010 Flash Crash, wash trading inflates crypto volume, and exchanges sold speed to HFTs. Agent-plus-Ghidra decompilation and cheap tick data mean one person can now audit the counterparty instead of guessing about it.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: This is game theory made practical: before you look for edge, measure the edge that's already being taken from you — your fills, the hours you hold, the apps you pay. It's defensive leverage, and it often turns into an offensive idea, like simply holding overnight.

manual_dives.title: Mocap as Reward — teaching cheap robots to move like you
manual_dives.thesis: The Microduck RL demo shows the classic failure: a loose reward function makes the robot 'stand' in a way nobody intended. The catalog also holds the fix, scattered across collections. FreeMoCap turns a webcam into markerless motion capture, HY-Motion produces motion from text on robot skeletons, and Blender plus a GPU contact solver can rehearse physical contact. Use captured or generated motion as an imitation reward on a cheap open robot. The reward-design trial and error becomes 'show it what you mean'.
manual_dives.why_it_matters: Hobby robotics is gated by reward engineering more than by hardware. A webcam reference clip gives an individual the motion-prior pipeline that only labs used to have, for small expressive robots, animatronics and installations.
manual_dives.novelty: The robotics entries and the motion and animation entries never reference each other. HY-Motion explicitly supports robot skeletons, yet it's filed as an animation tool. Nobody in the catalog points it at Microduck's reward-hacking problem.
